and, protection. This will be presented by Dr. coordinator of athletic training programs, and Derek Fairley, Ferry, our director of athletics and activities. Good afternoon. Thank you for your, your attention today, as we review Policy 8425. This is a new policy. It was, highlighted as a requirement under state

code, of-22-1271.9 and 22-1271.10. This is the establishment of safety standards t-to maintain, guidance reflective in the Virginia Department of Education and Virginia High School as it relates to exertional heat stroke and,

protection and prevention and recognition when we see a athlete in crisis. So as-- I wanna start off by telling you I'm, I'm appreciative that the Commonwealth, decided to exercise this in code. We've actually practiced this guidance since twenty twelve. Uh, we used to follow-- We were-- currently still we're following, recommendations from the Korey Stringer Institute. So since then, looking at the state

code, if you were to dive a little deeper into it, some of the things that they did is they, actually they're a little bit more conservative than we are, so we will definitely make sure we align, and you'll see that when we get into, the tiered, approach. Our-- Right now, if you walk onto any one of our LCPS high school campuses, you will already see that we have a banner that reflects, those current wet bulb protections and guidance that we have in place. So

you'll see there's a policy overview and framework. I, I'll just briefly discuss the reason for these are, is to protect, the health and the welfare of our students based on procedures to prevent, recognize, and respond to heat-related illnesses. This policy aligns with the Code of Virginia and the Virginia Department of Ed and, and the Virginia High School League. Heat safety protocols are strictly, based on wet bulb. Um, we used to use heat index years ago, but we all...

Each one of our athletic trainers carries a Kestler device, which is a device that measures wet bulb temperatures or wet bulb globe temperatures. Uh, we reassess every thirty minutes, during practice times, and our athletic trainers are the, the primary medical professional for-- re-responsible for monitoring and guiding, required practice modifications. And we are very blessed with the support of our school board to, to have two athletic trainers at each one of our schools.

So if you look at our tiered approach, what we used to modif-- used to follow the modifications under the guidance of the Korey Stringer Institute. And if you know, he was a famous football player who unfortunately succumbed to exertional heat stroke playing for the Minnesota Vikings. Um, so if you look tier one, tier two, they're very similar. The only difference is there's-- When it says a minimum of three water breaks, the,

it's the amount of water consumption. Um, four ounces is for tier one. Uh, six to eight ounces is in tier t- is, tier two. You'll see that in regulation later, but we're just talking about the policy today. As you see, when we hit these w-higher wet bulb temperatures in tier three, we remove helmets. That would be a football helmet, a baseball, softball, anything, any sport that requires a protective, headgear or

garment. Um, again, we're only keeping-- we're staying at the three mi-- three water breaks per hour. Again, water consumption, the amount of ounces is increased. We get to tier, four, that's where you're gonna see we're gonna take off no equipment for non-contact drills. That means we'll remove shoulder pads. We increase the water breaks to four per hour. As we get to tier five, no equipment.

You're in sh-- shirts and shorts. We're mainly talking about football in, in those instances. Lacrosse, towards the end of s-the spring season, you might see some of these temperatures rise to where we need to take these, these measures. And then we reduce the intensity of practices and, four hour-- four-- again, we'll stay with the four breaks. And then when we get to tier six, it, then we're, we're suspending all outdoor activities, and we're

moving to indoor sessions. Prevention, we talk about acclimation periods. We have out-of-season practices year-- I mean, our sports are year-round, so they are pretty much acclimated throughout the year. Um, but the, the big piece to the acclimation period, so in football, for example, the first three days are, are non-pads. Uh, the reason why is, is to allow an athlete to adjust to

the acclimation of the heat. And then day three, we can go helmet and shells, and shells would be a shoulder pad. Um, our cross-country programs, they typically have modified practices. The-- They don't go longer distances. We stay on campus as much as possible. Um, but we inten-- we increase the intensity th-through progression. So from, one week, they might be only running up to three or four miles, to by probably week three or four, you're

seeing five to seven-mile, day training re-regimens. Um, hydration, we, we provide, water at e-every one of our practices, and we provide shade when needed with either through a pop-up tent or through a team room, or we'll remove them and bring them inside to our athletic training room, which is a air-conditioned space. Uh, we can talk about cold water immersion. Uh, that is, something either we'll do through a,

a Rubbermaid tub, or we-- you sometimes you'll see what m-you-- we call a taco method, which is a tarp where you fill it with, coolers of ice and, water. There's also some other, apparatuses that you can purchase that will also, s-very similar. It almost looks like a, a sleeping bag, but it's, it's another type of cooling mechanism as well. Uh, so we cool first, transport

second. The most important thing is not to transport an athlete before they, before their temperature goes belowUm, 102. If it's, if it's, remaining above 102, we c-continue to cool until we can get them below 102, then we transport. That, that is the best practice, you know, th- we've-- unfortunately across the, the country, you've seen some, some alarming news where we've lost,

not, not LCPS, but there have been athletes who have succumbed to exertional heat stroke, and it's because m- usually it's because they transport too soon. Uh, so some of the things that you'll see here in the eli- when we talk about eligibility and training and return to play, we, we've been doing since, since two thousand and sixteen, we've been requiring our, every one of our coaches to go through the National Federation Heat Illness Prevention Course.

Um, this wasn't a guideline, or a mandate by the Virginia Department of Ed or the Virginia High School League. This was a proactive approach by us and the, the athletic trainers and athletic directors w- just, making sure we put layers of protection in, in place so our athletes are provided the most secure and protective environment that we can possibly pr-provide. mandatory, physical examination prior to being able to participate in any activity. post-emergency heat stroke recovery.
